title: Keychron's gaming mouse firmware is going open-source, while the company critiques 'firmware you can't read, can't audit, can't change'
summary: I'm always in favour of more open-source software.
body: Keychron, the gaming peripheral creator, has developed a name for itself as a defender of open-source software over the last few years. It has an entire ' Open Source Design Project ', where it posts access to files to customise its keyboards, and it even uses ZMK and QMK, which are open-source software for keyboards. Open-source mouse firmware has gone unloved by the company, until now. Keychron announced on X that it's currently developing ZGM, an open-source gaming mouse software for use with its mice. The company plans to launch ZGM at the start of 2027. Keychron says in the announcement, "Every gaming mouse on the market runs firmware you can't read, can't audit, can't change. So we built it ourselves." Alongside this, the company has published a new website , explaining the benefits of open-source gaming mouse firmware and how it came about. The new software is built on Zephyr ROTS and designed to be scalable and modular, meaning it can support multiple hardware variants and can work with unique sensors, buttons, and scroll wheels without rewriting. It's also designed with low-latency input in mind, and will support both wired and wireless mice. The benefit of it being open-…

title: Cooler Master V8 Ace 3DHP review
summary: Proving air coolers are still cool in 2026.
body: It's not often we see serious innovation in air cooling; many merely spin on tried and tested formulae. That's not the case here, however, as the Cooler Master V8 Ace 3DHP is offering something new to PC builders: 3DHP technology. I first glimpsed the 3DHP (3D Heat Pipe) tech in a backroom of Cooler Master's Taipei HQ in 2025. I was under a strict oath not to talk about anything I saw in that room, which was easy enough, as it was almost empty except for a pair of air coolers: one using a traditional U-shape heatpipe design and the other using 3DHP. The 3DHP design includes an additional heatpipe at the centre of the U-shape. The benefit of this extra heatpipe is clear through a thermal imaging camera: there's no deadzone (cool patch) in the middle of the cooler. For the V8 Ace, in particular, 3DHP is used on two of its six heatpipes—the two big ones in the middle—with the other four in a more traditional layout. Altogether, there are a lot of heatpipes running through every part of this single-tower cooler. That's the thing to remember when looking over the results from my testing with the V8 Ace 3DHP below. It's a single-tower cooler competing with the very best dual-tower coole…

title: AMD launches the RX 9050, and it's even more entry-level than expected - update: it's $279 and limited to certain regions
summary: Oh, and the 4 GB version is OEM-only.
body: AMD has launched a new graphics card, the RX 9050. This is an entry-level graphics card with a slim provision of cores and VRAM, more of a match for the 890M than the RX 9060. It's even more entry-level than initial rumours suggested, and while you'd hope for a great price to match, we're not getting our hopes up yet. Take a look at the specifications below, right from AMD's website, and you'll get an idea of the card. It's using the same Navi 44 GPU as the more capable entry-level and mid-range graphics cards, but it's been trimmed down to within an inch of its life. At 1,024 cores, it is actually a match for the 890M GPU found in Strix Point mobile chips, though it does have the big benefit of a desktop power budget, even if only 92 watts; RDNA 4 architecture, and 32 MB of Infinity Cache. It's also something that makes the creators of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 a little melancholy, per a recent interview with Automaton : "Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores," says CEO and Creative Director of Sandfall Interactive Guillaume Broche. title: Microsoft reportedly using TPM chips to weed out Windows piracy
summary: Spare a thought for the system administrators.
body: Microsoft's Trusted Platform Module, specifically TPM 2.0, has been part of Windows 11's system requirements since the operating system's introduction in 2021 . Now that the TPM is ubiquitous, being included with most CPUs for many years, Microsoft is looking to leverage it "to activate Windows devices at scale." Currently, the enterprise sector activates Windows via Microsoft's Key Management Service (KMS), but according to the Windows IT Pro Blog , "modern organizations increasingly require stronger assurances around device identity and activation integrity." Basically, hackers can already clone or fake KMS server software, so the TPM is intended to provide a hardware-level security check to curb this. The blog post then very briefly breaks down how TPM attestation works. Essentially, the KMS host flashes its TPM credentials to prove its hardware identity. These TPM credentials also reveal whether the KMS host has been tampered with or not, and Microsoft checks these before it allows the host to activate any devices. When everything appears to be in order, the KMS host will be allowed to "securely serve activation requests for Windows devices in the organization." Microsoft goes…

title: AI companies are anonymously buying and destroying millions of books through middleman services to avoid headlines about AI companies buying and destroying millions of books
summary: Booksellers say they're facing a sudden surge of orders for seemingly random rare books—and fear they might be profiting from their destruction.
body: AI isn't doing great on the PR front. Whether it's the exponentially increasing electricity consumption amidst worsening climate change, the data centers leaking toxic pollutants into neighboring communities, or the years-long parade of business leaders insisting the technology will replace humans in "most, if not all" professional fields, the AI industry has an excellent record of inspiring resentment and contempt. And, it seems, the AI companies know it. New reporting from 404 Media suggests that, in an effort to shield themselves from the PR fallout of their data harvesting, major AI providers have turned to third-party middleman services to anonymously source the physical books they've been stripping for training data at an industrial scale—and destroying in the process. (Image credit: Cheng Xin via Getty Images) In an information ecosystem increasingly poisoned by regurgitated and recirculated AI slop, untainted samples of quality written text have, ironically, only become more valuable for the companies making them so hard to find. The AI model arms race requires an ever-widening set of training data, making physical books that predate the proliferation of LLM-generated text…

title: Don't let this beautifully-drawn action RPG starring two girls trained in Sekiro-style combat get lost in the sea of new games on Steam
summary: Lunarium has the atmosphere of Nier with the satisfying action of a soulslike.
body: Do me a favor and don't let Lunarium get lost in the sea of game releases on Steam. Tons of action RPGs show up in my inbox and it's sometimes hard to differentiate which one is which. Lunarium stood out mostly because of its art style, which sort of looks like it would fit on the cover of a Nier or Final Fantasy game. And then I played it and discovered one of the best action RPGs of the year. The last thing I want is for a game with such an evocative, hand-drawn style to get swallowed up by the tidal wave of Steam games that try to fake it with generative AI . Lunarium's crumbling ruins and overgrown forests are like a Nier: Automata level squished down into an isometric 2D perspective. It's a sad game with a world painted in muted colors, as if the dark monsters you encounter are draining the life out of it. Lunarium sort of plays like a soulslike, but it's much closer to Sekiro than Dark Souls in terms of pacing. Dying will respawn all the enemies, but you can dispatch them (or skip them entirely) to get back to where you were in no time. title: OpenAI CEO thinks the AI singularity is already upon us and that cracking down on it wouldn't be good for humanity, because of course he does

body: Tech leaders sure do say some wacky things. But AI tech leaders perhaps say the wackiest things (here's looking at you, Palantir CEO ). Not one to be outdone, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman recently had a sit-down with YouTuber Relentless where he shared that he's not only hopeful for the AI singularity, but believes it's already upon us. He says, "We are now, like in the singularity, like this is the moment". Altman continues, "10 years ago this was like a kind of far-off dream at best. It seemed very improbable, and now we're like, actually in the moment that we used to talk about at the lunch table in a very not serious way." For those of you who aren't into science fiction, the singularity refers to the moment where the growth of robots (or in this case, AI) has surpassed human control or human intelligence (in this case, the latter). Effectively, the moment where you can't exactly put the genie back in the bottle. Altman seems to believe that generative AI has already become so powerful that it's surpassing human intelligence. On Tuesday, local investigators searched both Chang's residence as well as their desk in Nvidia's Taipei office. Nvidia itself has not been accused of any wrongdoing, though Chang faces allegations of breach of trust and forgery. Chang's detainment was carried out as part of a larger investigation into the alleged smuggling of AI chips into China. According to Bloomberg , this is just one investigation of at least eight similar probes into potential smuggling routes across four different jurisdictions. Taiwanese prosecutors allege that the defendants had already smuggled chips into China via Japan previously. title: Chinese company reportedly building its own DUV chipmaking machines, and that's a really big deal
summary: Meanwhile, the US still hopes to block ASML from selling and servicing similar machines in China.
body: A Chinese state-backed company has begun mass producing deep ultraviolet lithography machines, reports The Information . That's a big step towards China's semiconductor biz standing on its own two feet. It takes a complicated lithographic machine to produce a modern chip, and there are two main types: EUV (Extreme Ultraviolet Lithography) and DUV (Deep Ultraviolet Lithography). It's the older of the two, DUV, that a Chinese company is said to have figured out. These sorts of immersion machines are still used for modern computer chips, and today most are made by Dutch company ASML, which took over from the Japanese companies that dominated prior. Citing people familiar with the matter, The Information says the Chinese DUV machines are set to be delivered to customers this year . Customers including, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp., Hua Hong Semiconductor, and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT). Yeah, that same CXMT everyone is talking about due to surging memory costs. While this does challenge ASML for the sale of DUV machines in China, the machines are said to be lagging behind in performance and reliability. This news comes at a time when a plan to restrict sale…
